record.paper_title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation
record.original_question: For a cancer patient who may be eligible for either aggressive continuous therapy aimed at cure or adaptive therapy aimed at long-term containment, how should clinicians and modelers decide between treat-to-cure and treat-to-contain strategies before treatment begins? What disease characteristics, eco-evolutionary factors, biomarkers, resistant-cell frequencies, competition and tradeoffs, tumor burden, toxicity, quality of life, and practical monitoring constraints are needed to stratify patients into a continuous-therapy cohort versus an adaptive-therapy cohort, especially because a failed curative attempt can leave too many resistant cancer cells for later adaptive control?

evidence.quote: An explicit goal of adaptive therapy is to turn cancer into a chronic disease with sporadic (but life-long) management. Taking this approach likely means abandoning the hope of cure.
But is identifying such patients prior to treatment even possible?

So how does one decide between these opposing strategies? What key disease characteristics are needed to stratify patients into a treat-to-cure cohort (using continuous therapies) versus a treat-to-contain cohort (using adaptive therapies) [58]?
Cure or control could be favored depdending on the patient, the disease state, and the drugs used.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a mathematical model of a tumor consisting of two competing subpopulations: sensitive cells of density S(t) and resistant cells of density R(t), evolving under a Lotka–Volterra-type dynamic

    dS/dt = r_S S (1 - (S + a_{SR} R)/K) - d(u(t)) S,
    dR/dt = r_R R (1 - (R + a_{RS} S)/K),

where r_S, r_R > 0 are intrinsic growth rates, a_{SR}, a_{RS} > 0 are competition coefficients, K > 0 is the carrying capacity, and u(t) ∈ [0, u_max] is the drug dose with d(·) a non-decreasing kill function acting only on sensitive cells. Assume an initial state (S_0, R_0) with R_0 ≥ 1 (at least one resistant cell). Two treatment strategies are considered:

  (i) Continuous (treat-to-cure) therapy: u(t) ≡ u_max until S(t) + R(t) falls below a detection threshold ε; success is defined as eradication, i.e. S(t) + R(t) = 0 in finite time.

  (ii) Adaptive (treat-to-contain) therapy: u(t) is chosen as a feedback control of the observable total burden N(t) = S(t) + R(t) (e.g., on/off switching at thresholds N_on, N_off), with the objective of keeping N(t) bounded for all t ≥ 0 while maximizing a quality-of-life functional Q[u].

Problem. Identify a decidable, model-based stratification rule — i.e., a measurable function

    Φ : (r_S, r_R, a_{SR}, a_{RS}, K, S_0, R_0, d(·), toxicity parameters, monitoring noise σ) ⟼ {cure, contain},

based only on pre-treatment observables (such as tumor burden, estimated resistant-cell frequency R_0/(S_0+R_0), competition coefficients inferred from biomarkers, and bounds on the kill function), such that:

  (a) Whenever Φ outputs "cure", strategy (i) achieves eradication with probability at least 1 - α under the stochastic version of the model with monitoring noise σ;
  (b) Whenever Φ outputs "contain", strategy (ii) keeps E[N(t)] bounded for all t and achieves expected quality-of-life Q strictly larger than that achievable by (i) following a failed curative attempt (i.e., the residual resistant population after (i) is too large to be contained);
  (c) The rule Φ is optimal in the sense that no other pre-treatment decision rule, using the same observables, achieves a strictly better trade-off between cure probability, expected survival time, and Q.

Determine whether such a stratification rule Φ exists, characterize the regions of parameter space (in terms of resistant-cell frequency, competitive ability of resistant cells, drug efficacy, and tumor burden) on which each output is optimal, and exhibit explicit thresholds separating the "treat-to-cure" and "treat-to-contain" regimes.
artifact.status_search_result: This question of pre-treatment stratification between curative and containment (adaptive therapy) strategies is highlighted as an open clinical and mathematical-modeling question in recent surveys on adaptive therapy. While various Lotka–Volterra and game-theoretic models have proposed candidate criteria (e.g., resistant-cell fraction, competition strength), no universally validated stratification rule has been established as of 2026.
